title: Desire as the enemy (3.30–3.43)
hook: Arjuna asks why people do what they know is wrong, as if pushed by force, and Krishna names the enemy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the example of the wise: whatever the best do, others do, so even Krishna keeps working. Your line was lead by doing. What did someone see you do? Today, the end of chapter three. Day one hundred seventy.

Ten minutes after the text someone swore they wouldn't send, a small question shows up: why did I do that? I knew better. The same question follows the third helping, the thing said in anger, the app opened again at midnight. It's as if something else had its hands on the wheel. Near the end of chapter three, Arjuna asks exactly this. What pushes a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against their own will, as if forced? Krishna's answer is short, and it names two things.
screen: `WHY DID I DO THAT?` → `SOMETHING ELSE AT THE WHEEL.` → `ARJUNA ASKS IT TOO.`

segments.voice: First Krishna gathers up the chapter. Offer all your actions to me, he says, and fight free of fever. Then verse thirty-five. Shreyan svadharmo vigunah, paradharmat svanushthitat. Better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Do your own work, even clumsily; someone else's path, however well walked, is full of fear. Then Arjuna's question, in Sanskrit: atha kena prayukto 'yam papam charati purushah. Then, by what is a person driven to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? And Krishna's answer: kama esha krodha esha. It is desire. It is anger. Born of restlessness, the quality called rajas. All-devouring, and the great wrong. Know this, he says, as the enemy. Then three pictures of how it hides. As fire is covered by smoke. As a mirror is covered by dust. As a baby is covered by the womb. The light is still there. You just can't see it. This enemy, he says, is like a fire that's never satisfied. And he tells you where it lives: in the senses, the mind and the understanding. It uses them to cloud what you know. So he gives an order of strength. The senses are powerful. The mind is higher than the senses. The understanding is higher than the mind. And higher than understanding is the self. Knowing that, steady yourself by the self, and then: jahi shatrum mahabaho kamarupam durasadam. Strike down, mighty-armed one, this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome. That's chapter three. The action was never the problem. The grasping is.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · `WHAT DRIVES US, AS IF FORCED?` · `DESIRE AND ANGER: THE ENEMY.` · `SMOKE, DUST, THE WOMB.` · then, large: `STRIKE DOWN THE ENEMY CALLED DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wipe the mirror. Settle, and breathe. Picture a mirror covered in a fine layer of dust. That's how a strong want sits over what you already know. Now think of one thing you do even though you know better. Name the want underneath it, plainly: I want comfort, I want to be right, I want more. Don't fight it. Just see it for what it is. And each time you breathe out, picture one slow wipe across the glass. Behind the dust, the mirror was always clear. The bell holds the time.
Desire as the enemy. What drives us to act against what we know: desire and anger, hiding like smoke over fire, dust over a mirror.
Your line: know the enemy. Today, when you're about to do the thing you know you shouldn't, stop and name the want out loud. Then choose. Day one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Gita 3.35, better one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well, and 3.37, naming desire and anger as the enemy, are verses some Hindus learn by heart and return to when facing a hard choice.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you've noticed people do wrong even when they don't want to, as if forced. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he asks: by what is a person driven to do wrong, even unwillingly? Krishna answers: desire and anger. know this as the enemy.

original.note: Sanskrit: desire. in Gita 3.37, named with anger as the enemy.

trapdoor: what you thought: wanting things is bad.
what it means: the grasping kind of desire clouds what you know, like smoke on fire or dust on a mirror. the self behind it is higher and clear.
what a scholar hears: kama is also one of the four aims of life, rightly pursued; here the Gita names its grasping form, born of rajas, as the enemy.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they did and no longer opens on 'You've done it'; fixed 'answers in one word' (the answer names two things, desire and anger); cut the unsourced 'held on to for centuries' and 'most human question' and the 'most quoted verses' claim in howItsDone.
3.35 'another's dharma is fraught with fear (bhayavahah)'. Paraphrased. Confirm.
3.42 hierarchy: senses, manas, buddhi, and 'He' (the self). Confirm.
Trapdoor mentions kama as one of the purusharthas; confirm this nuance is welcome here.
Chapter 3 close. Chapter 3.31–34 (those who follow/reject the teaching; acting according to nature) summarized or omitted. Confirm.
